title: How would you estimate what people in the UK spend on umbrellas each year?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "What do people in the UK spend on umbrellas each year?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: This looks trivial, but it tests whether you can turn a vague habit (how often do people really buy an umbrella?) into a defensible number. Have a go at your own estimate before reading on.
body:
The question

What do people in the UK spend on umbrellas each year?

The approach

People × umbrellas bought per year × average price.

Tip: Round to friendly numbers and say that you are rounding. Nobody expects decimals.

Step by step

  1. People in the UK: 68M
  2. × 0.33 umbrellas each per year (one every 3 years)
  3. × £10 average price

That gives about £227M a year.

Does it make sense?

Around £3 per person per year: small, which fits an item people rarely think about.

Real-world check

The UK population was about 69.3 million at mid-2024 (ONS). This example rounds to 68 million, which is fine: in an interview, any sensible round number is accepted as long as you say it.

Source: ONS: UK population estimates, mid-2024.

Split replacement and first-time demand

The estimate treats each person as buying roughly one umbrella every three years. That is reasonable as a starting model, but not everyone buys at the same rate. A frequent train commuter may replace a lost umbrella every year; a person who mostly drives may buy one much less often.

For a sensitivity check, replace the assumed annual purchase rate of 0.33 with 0.25. Using 68 million people and £10 each gives £170 million a year, compared with about £227 million in the original calculation. A seemingly modest behavioural difference changes the market by roughly a quarter.

Ask whether the client is interested in units, retail spending or manufacturer revenue. A £10 umbrella bought in a shop does not create £10 of revenue for the manufacturer. Sales through tourist outlets and travel hubs may also be unusually seasonal.
